items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: No. Actually I never thought about it until Duke Ellington died... So that’s what actually triggered me. I think in my case it was Duke Ellington, that memoir, written by Nat Hentoff.

ctx.x: That’s an interesting statement. I mean you certainly made an impact and kept that tradition alive. You know when you read about your music, most people mention that it brings in a whole other area of influence from your native culture. And when you write do you consciously try to think of things from your youth that are now combined with American jazz, or is it just kind of part of you?

No. Actually I never thought about it until Duke Ellington died. Before that, you know it was just a Japanese traditional concept, or being Japanese playing jazz was some sort of a handicap. When I was growing up in Japan as a player, they always said that Filipino people have better feeling than Japanese, and indeed the Filipino players played better than us, and it’s simply because they have a longer history. They weren’t under — they were colonized by America so they are more exposed for jazz, much longer than…

So that has been going on for a long time. When Duke Ellington died, it was ’73, or ’74 I think, and there was a Village Voice, Nat Hentoff had a memoir. items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Duke died. ... Duke was always very uh, … grandeur. He came a couple of times to the [Berklee] school when I was at school, and I had a terrible cold. And he would say [deep, elegant voice], “Oh, poor child. My dear, I have to send you to my doctor.”

ctx.x: But 50 cents, so I said, “Well, that‟s, we can afford it.” That‟s how it started in 1973, spring. And he got all the musicians, and it was a … took about six months to settle down. Some musicians didn‟t want to put up with the music; some musicians, I didn‟t think were appropriate, you know, so on, blah, blah, blah. So that‟s how the band started, not as a working band. It was just to get together and so on, and I thought if I could probably develop my repertoire and I was kind of getting my, more and more … it‟s…
